title: Handling Sum Queries After Update
description: Brute force to optimized: flipping every bit and re-summing directly versus a lazy-propagation segment tree using the length-minus-count flip identity.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given a binary array nums1, an integer array nums2, and a list of queries, process each query: type [1, l, r] flips every bit in nums1 from index l to r, inclusive; type [2, p, 0] adds (sum of nums1) times p to every element of nums2 conceptually, but really just adds that amount to a running total sum of nums2; type [3, 0, 0] asks for the current total sum of nums2. Return the answers to every type-3 query, in order.

blocks.text: Maintain a binary array nums1 that can have ranges flipped (0 becomes 1, 1 becomes 0), while tracking a running total (starting as the sum of nums2) that grows by p times the current count of 1s in nums1 whenever a type-2 query occurs, and answer the running total whenever asked.

blocks.title: Analogy: Toggling Light Switches in Sections and Tracking Cumulative Energy Use
blocks.text: Picture a row of light switches, where a query can flip every switch in a range at once, and separately, a running energy meter increases by (number of currently ON switches) times some rate whenever asked. Flipping a whole SECTION of switches at once, without touching each individually, is the key efficiency needed.

blocks.caption: A segment tree tracks the count of 1s per range; flipping is O(1) per touched node via a lazy flag

blocks.text: Flipping index 1 makes nums1 = [1,1,1] (3 ones). The type-2 query adds 3 times 1 = 3 to the running total (starting at 0). The type-3 query returns 3.

Before flipping every bit in a range directly, notice a key identity: flipping a range of length L containing c ones turns it into L minus c ones, letting a segment tree update the "ones count" for an entire range in O(1), deferring the actual per-bit flip with a lazy flag.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Flipping a range does not require inspecting each bit individually; if a range of length L currently has c ones, after flipping it has exactly L minus c ones.

Observation 2: A segment tree node covering a range can update its stored "ones count" using this identity in O(1), and mark a lazy "pending flip" flag instead of recursing into its children immediately.

Observation 3: That lazy flag is only pushed down to children when the segment tree needs to look inside that range more precisely (partial overlap during a query or update).

Observation 4: The total count of ones in nums1 is always available at the root in O(1), letting a type-2 query add (root's ones count) times p to the running total instantly.
This leads to a segment tree over nums1, tracking the count of ones per range with lazy propagation for range flips, letting both range-flip and total-ones queries run in O(log n) or better.
Maintain nums1 as a plain array. On a type-1 query, flip every bit in the range directly. On a type-2 query, re-sum nums1 from scratch to get the current ones count.

items: Type 1 [l, r]: flip every bit in nums1 from l to r directly.
Type 2 [p]: sum all of nums1 directly to get the ones count, and add ones count times p to the running total.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every type-1 query flips each bit in its range one at a time.
Every type-2 query re-sums the entire array to find the current ones count, regardless of how much (or little) has changed since the last query.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n) per type-1 or type-2 query in the worst case; O(1) per type-3 query.
Space: O(n).
Limitation: both flipping a range and re-summing the whole array touch every element directly; with up to 100000 queries on an array of up to 100000 elements, this can reach 10 billion operations.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why touching every bit is unnecessary: a segment tree node covering a range only needs to know its CURRENT COUNT of ones to update it after a flip, using the identity new count equals range length minus old count, no per-bit inspection required.

How lazy propagation helps: a pending flip on a range can be recorded as a flag on the segment tree node covering exactly that range, deferring the actual per-child update until it is truly needed (a query or update that only partially overlaps that range).

How the total ones count stays available instantly: the segment tree's root always stores the count of ones across the entire array, updated correctly by every flip operation, giving O(1) access for type-2 queries.

The core idea: a segment tree over nums1, tracking ones-count per range with lazy-flip propagation, giving O(log n) range flips and O(1) total-ones lookups.

Build a segment tree over nums1, where each node stores the count of ones in its range. On a range flip, for any node fully contained in the flip range, update its count directly (range length minus current count) and mark a lazy flip flag, without recursing further; push that flag down only when a later operation needs to look inside that range more precisely. On a type-2 query, read the root's ones count (all of nums1) in O(1) and add it times p to the running total.

The identity "flipping a range of length L with c ones gives L minus c ones" lets any fully-covered segment tree node update its stored count in O(1), without visiting its children; the lazy flag defers that same update to children until it is genuinely needed. Since the root always reflects the true total ones count across all of nums1, type-2 queries read it directly in O(1), and type-1 queries only ever touch O(log n) nodes per flip.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(log n) per type-1 query, O(1) per type-2 or type-3 query.
Space: O(n) for the segment tree.

blocks.text: Stating the core identity, "flipping turns count into length minus count," up front is the key insight that justifies the entire lazy-propagation segment tree design.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "how do you flip a whole range without touching every bit", think: a segment tree node's ones-count becomes its length minus its count, applied in O(1) with a lazy flag deferring the deeper update.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force runs type-1 and type-2 queries in O(n) time. The optimized lazy-propagation segment tree runs type-1 in O(log n) and type-2/type-3 in O(1). Both use O(n) space.

items: Pattern: a lazy-propagation segment tree, using the flip identity (count becomes length minus count).
Core Idea: maintain a segment tree tracking ones-count per range; flip a range in O(log n) using the length-minus-count identity with a lazy flag; read the total ones count instantly from the root.
Time: O(n) per flip or re-sum for the brute force, O(log n) per flip and O(1) per total-ones lookup for the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: flipping a range only needs its current ones-count, not a per-bit inspection, letting an entire covered node update in O(1).
Interview Difficulty: a substantial lazy-propagation segment tree implementation, testing careful push-down logic.
One line memory trick: lazy segment tree; flip count becomes length minus count, root holds the grand total.
